analysis.one_liner: Raises pay, recruitment, and layoff rules for companies using H-1B guest workers, and cuts the visa stay to three years.
analysis.headline: The bill never came up for action: it was introduced with zero cosponsors, referred to an immigration subcommittee on January 28, 1997, and died there when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have tightened the rules for employers who hire H-1B guest workers in specialty jobs. Companies would have to pay foreign hires at least the full actual or prevailing wage, swear they had not laid off U.S. workers in the same job recently, show they tried in good faith to hire an American first, and pay higher fines for misrepresenting any of it. Employers that rely heavily on H-1B workers would face extra steps to recruit and train U.S. workers, including payments into a training fund. The allowed stay on the visa would drop from six years to three, and workers would have to keep a residence abroad.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. workers in fields where employers use H-1B hires, especially technology and engineering: the bill's full-wage requirement removes the discount employers could take against the prevailing wage, its layoff and recruitment attestations make it harder to pass over available American workers, and higher penalties give the rules teeth. U.S. college students would also gain, because employers dependent on H-1B labor would have to fund scholarships and training for Americans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. workers competing with H-1B hires

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to pay H-1B workers 100 percent of the actual wage or the prevailing wage, whichever applies, up from the 95 percent floor then in law, and offer the same benefits given to comparable U.S. workers [S3].

Employers would have to attest they had not laid off or displaced any U.S. worker in the same occupation in the prior six months, and would not do so in the 90 days around the petition, covering workers obtained through contractors and temp agencies [S3].
Before filing, an employer would have to attempt in good faith to recruit a U.S. worker for the job at full wage and benefits [S3].

Misrepresentation penalties would rise from $1,000 to $5,000 per violation, with petition bans of at least one year, five years for repeat willful violations, and double the backpay added for willful violations [S3].

Employers dependent on H-1B workers would have to take effective steps to hire and train Americans, including paying into a certified fund for scholarships and worker training, and could not charge those costs to the foreign worker [S3].
The maximum stay for H-1B workers would drop from six years to three years, and holders would have to maintain a residence abroad they do not intend to abandon [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that hire H-1B workers, particularly technology companies and staffing firms that place contract workers at other companies. They would pay higher wages, face stricter recruitment and layoff restrictions, pay fines up to five times higher for misrepresentation, and, if heavily dependent on H-1B labor, pay 5 to 10 percent of each foreign hire's compensation into a training fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: H-1B employers and IT staffing firms

drawbacks.text: Employers argue that H-1B visas fill genuine shortages of specialized skills, and that tighter rules would make it harder and slower to hire needed workers, raising compliance costs especially for small firms that could be flagged as dependent after just four H-1B hires [S3].

Cutting the allowed stay from six years to three, combined with the foreign-residence requirement, would shorten the runway for workers already in the pipeline and could push companies to move work offshore rather than hire in the United States [S3].

The training-fund payments amount to a new levy of 5 to 10 percent of a foreign hire's compensation on dependent employers, a cost that would fall on the industry and could be passed into prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have meaningfully shifted bargaining power toward U.S. workers in tech occupations by closing the 95-percent wage discount, policing layoffs and recruitment, and giving penalties real teeth. The honest cost is higher friction and expense for employers, some of which may translate into slower hiring or offshoring rather than more jobs for Americans; the dependence rules also hit small firms early, at four H-1B employees. On balance the protections for workers are direct and the compliance burden is concentrated on a specific industry.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee's immigration subcommittee from late January 1997 until the Congress ended in January 1999, never getting a hearing vote or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers of Michigan introduced the bill on January 7, 1997, the opening day of the 105th Congress [S1][S3][S5].
No member joined as a cosponsor [S4].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on January 7, 1997, and to the Subcommittee on Immigration and Claims on January 28, 1997; no further action was ever recorded [S1][S5].
The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that hire H-1B workers, especially technology companies and staffing firms, came out ahead: no full-wage requirement, no layoff or recruitment attestations, penalties stayed at $1,000, and the six-year visa stay remained in place.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MI), bill sponsor and ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 105th Congress and gave introductory remarks [S1][S3][S5].

against.name: House Subcommittee on Immigration and Claims
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Judiciary Committee with first referral of the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 28, 1997 and recorded no hearings, markups, or votes on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Rep. Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; the committee never brought it to a markup or vote [S5].

against.name: Information technology employers
against.role: Industry groups for companies reliant on H-1B hiring
against.what_they_did: Pressed Congress in this period to expand, not restrict, the H-1B program; Congress instead raised the visa cap in 1998 while restrictions like this bill went nowhere.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split was ever recorded [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Technology employers that hire H-1B workers
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to pay foreign hires at least the full actual or prevailing wage, banned hiring them right after laying off U.S. workers in the same job, required good-faith recruitment of Americans first, and raised misrepresentation fines from $1,000 to $5,000 with multi-year petition bans. Those costs came directly out of savings employers gained by paying below-market wages to visa-dependent workers.

Firms that place H-1B contract workers at client companies would have to make every client sign an attestation to the same wage and layoff rules, and could be held liable for client failures. Heavily H-1B-dependent staffing firms would also owe 5 to 10 percent of each hire's compensation into a training fund for U.S. students and workers.

Employers dependent on H-1B labor would have to fund scholarships and graduate fellowships for U.S. citizen and permanent-resident students in relevant fields, channeling industry money into American higher education.
